articles.title: Latest 2027 Men's NCAA Tournament Bracket Projections
articles.summary: College basketball's Feast Week is already in full swing, and the potential NCAA tournament ramifications have been resplendent.
articles.body:
College basketball's Feast Week is already in full swing, and the potential NCAA tournament ramifications have been resplendent.

The Houston Cougars made the biggest positive impression of the past week by winning the Players Era 8. (Not to be confused with the Players Era 16, which begins on Tuesday.) They surged all the way to our new No. 1 overall seed, in part because each team that was on our No. 1 seed line one week ago suffered a loss in the past seven days.

The Baha Mar Championship has also already concluded. Seton Hall vaulted into our projected field by winning that four-team event, while Wisconsin went straight from a No. 9 seed to the wrong side of the cut line by going 0-2 in that event.

And though it wasn't part of a neutral-site tournament, Illinois going on the road and blowing out Duke sure did shake up the seed list, with the Illini vaulting back up to a No. 1 seed while the Blue Devils fell to the No. 6 seed line. (Which, frankly, might still be too generous.)

Before we go any further, please note that the first NET rankings of the 2026-27 season won't be released until Dec. 7. As such, all talk of "Quads" records and other metrics-based arguments is on hold for another two weeks. It's mostly vibes in November, but we do have a pretty good idea of which wins are big enough that we'll still be talking about them in mid-March.

With that in mind, here is our latest glance into the Selection Sunday crystal ball.

Later in the season, automatic bids will be determined by conference record. For now, they are determined by KenPom ranking.

Also, please forgive any first-round pairings which are rematches of scheduled nonconference games. We won't start worrying about avoiding those until shortly after Feast Week.

Hard to imagine there's any argument against Houston at No. 1 overall after the Cougars improved to 6-0 by taking down former projected No. 1 seeds Florida and Kansas.

Sorting out Nos. 2-7, on the other hand, is a bit tricky at this early juncture.

As the only undefeated team of the bunch—not to mention a team that stomped Arkansas in Washington D.C., before also winning a true road game over Maryland—Virginia stands apart from the crowd a bit as the best candidate for No. 2 overall. We'll feel even better about Virginia as a No. 1 seed seven days from now if they also take care of business against both Marquette and Xavier in Nassau this week.

Considering Florida did beat both Notre Dame and West Virginia as bookends to the loss to Houston, it's hard to justify dropping the Gators any further than two spots to No. 3 overall.

And after what Illinois did to Duke in Cameron Indoor Stadium, it would just feel wrong to not have the Illini on the top line due to a close road loss to Texas Tech.

Arizona, Kansas and Connecticut each present compelling one-loss cases of their own, though. Even though Arizona's loss to UCLA was the least forgivable of the bunch, slight edge to the Wildcats as the top No. 2 seed because of the combination of their head-to-head victory over UConn and their road win at Auburn.

Already, though, the debate is getting fun. It's been great to see all of these upper-echelon teams loading up on quality tests just three weeks into the campaign.

10 Words on Each of the 10 'Bubbliest' Teams

Fifth-to-Last In : Virginia Tech Hokies—Needs bounce back from no-showing against Oklahoma State on Sunday.

Fourth-to-Last In : Providence Friars—Win over VCU in Maui might be discussed all season.

Third-to-Last In : Creighton Bluejays—Hanging in there, but let's see after Players Era 16.

Second-to-Last In : Seton Hall Pirates—Winning Baha Mar Championship propels Seton Hall into the field.

Last Team In : Wichita State Shockers—That 25-point beatdown of New Mexico was a real eye-opener.

First Team Out : TCU Horned Frogs—Best win of season was a home game against Milwaukee.

Second Team Out : Saint Louis Billikens—Two consecutive losses by at least 10 points? Not great!

Third Team Out : Wisconsin Badgers—Drops like a lead balloon after two losses in Nassau.

Fourth Team Out : Santa Clara Broncos—Blew a commanding lead in a heartbreaking loss to VCU.

Fifth Team Out : Xavier Musketeers—Had to drop them out after getting smoked by Iowa.

Ranking Top 9 Players to Watch in MCBB 👀

8 Teams in the Projected Field : 2. Virginia, 23. Duke, 24. Louisville, 25. Miami (FL), 40. Pittsburgh, 46. North Carolina, 48. Notre Dame, 51. Virginia Tech

Also Considered : Florida State, NC State, SMU

Pretty much no matter what happened on Tuesday night when Illinois visited Duke, we were going to come away from that game with some real concerns about a two-loss team that opened the season ranked in the AP Top 3.

That said, we never could have guessed it would be a full-blown panic about the Blue Devils after one of their worst home losses in at least half a century.

Illinois' Andrej Stojakovic scored 46 points. Quentin Coleman also put on one heck of a show. And Duke just generally looked helpless and dispassionate in a 99-78 beatdown.

The Blue Devils proceeded to struggle with Washington State late Saturday night in California, but did at least avoid taking what would have been an even more disastrous loss. However, it's the next two that really matter: against Connecticut in Las Vegas on Wednesday and at Florida next Tuesday.

Win those two and everyone will somewhat forget about the poor showings against Michigan State, Illinois and Washington State.

Conversely, Duke could easily lose both of those games and would be 4-4 (or worse) through eight games for the first time since 1982—two years before Mike Krzyzewski's first NCAA tournament appearance.

Meanwhile, how about those Pitt Panthers?

They smoked Villanova by 20 behind a 31-point, 14-rebound masterpiece from Baye Ndongo, who is now averaging north of 20 and 10 for the year. Pitt also blew out Central Michigan this week in improving to 6-0.

We shall see if it lasts. The Panthers were also 6-0 with a couple of quality wins early in the 2024-25 campaign, only to go 11-15 the rest of the way and miss the Dance.

Hard to argue with the early returns, though, as Pitt enters the projected field as a No. 10 seed.

9 Teams in the Projected Field : 1. Houston, 5. Arizona, 6. Kansas, 10. Texas Tech, 19. BYU, 20. Iowa State, 30. Baylor, 39. West Virginia, 50. Cincinnati

Also Considered : Oklahoma State, TCU, Arizona State

Biggest Development : Houston Wins Players Era 8

The Players Era 8 field consisted of three title contenders (Houston, Florida and Kansas), three likely tournament teams (Auburn, West Virginia and Notre Dame), one "home" team that figured to be a tough out in Las Vegas (UNLV) and one Rutgers (Rutgers).

Whoever went 3-0 in that event was inevitably going to earn a lot of respect.

And though Houston was nowhere near as laughably dominant as Michigan was in winning its three games in last year's Players Era Festival by a combined margin of 110 points, the Cougars sure did make a statement in running through Rutgers, Florida and Kansas with some room to spare en route to becoming our new No. 1 overall seed.

The star of that show was Kelvin Sampson's new point guard, Dedan Thomas Jr.

Thomas got pretty much whatever he wanted from Florida, finishing with 30 points against what had been the No. 1 team in the AP poll. He proceeded to rack up 16 points, eight assists and three steals in the championship game against Kansas. Not going to find many two-game stretches (let alone in two days) more impressive than that this season.

Houston should cruise through its next four home games (Oakland, Queens, Central Arkansas and Texas State) before taking a 10-0 record up against Alabama at Madison Square Garden on Dec. 7.

While Houston ascended to No. 1 overall, TCU exited stage right following its home loss to Texas A&M. Robbie Avila had 10 points and four rebounds in his Horned Frogs debut, but TCU squandered a big early lead on its way to an overtime loss.

It wasn't a terrible resume loss, but it does bring the Horned Frogs to 0-1 against teams in the KenPom top 275. We can do better than that around the bubble, even with eight more spots to fill.

8 Teams in the Projected Field : 7. Connecticut, 15. St. John's, 36. Villanova, 47. Georgetown, 49. Marquette, 52. Providence, 53. Creighton, 54. Seton Hall

Biggest Development : Seton Hall Wins Baha Mar Championship

The four-team field for the Baha Mar Championship wasn't exactly a murderers' row, but Wisconsin, NC State, Seton Hall and Murray State all entered that event rated in the Nos. 50-80 range on KenPom.

In other words: Bubble ramifications galore.

And after a competitive loss at Alabama the previous week, Seton Hall was the big winner in Nassau, taking down the Badgers in the first game before outlasting the Wolfpack in overtime in the championship.

In both games, the Pirates' bench was huge. Reserves combined for 94 of their 161 points, led by Trey Parker's 21 against Wisconsin before Rodney Brown (24) and Terry Copeland Jr. (22) carried them against NC State.

Coincidentally, it was a win over NC State during Feast Week that put Seton Hall on the map a bit last year, too, then improving to 6-0 with an upset of the Wolfpack in the first round of the Maui Invitational.

However, after starting out 14-2 and even briefly making it into the AP Top 25, the Pirates cratered during Big East play and weren't all that close to making the Dance in the end.

For the time being, though, let's entertain the possibility that this team is gearing up to dance in its fifth season under Shaheen Holloway.

10 Teams in the Projected Field : 4. Illinois, 8. Michigan State, 14. UCLA, 16. Nebraska, 22. Indiana, 26. USC, 28. Minnesota, 32. Michigan, 35. Ohio State, 41. Iowa

Biggest Development : Indiana's Best Week Since...?

Neither John Calipari's current team nor his former team is anywhere near as good as we envisioned them to be before the season began.

Still, Indiana scoring a five-point win over Arkansas (in NYC) followed by a 14-point win over Kentucky (in Indianapolis) was a mighty impressive one-two punch.

Against the Razorbacks, the Hoosiers rallied from a late four-point deficit behind the strength of Duke transfer Darren Harris. They drained triples on three straight possessions, Harris making the first two and finding Bryce Lindsay for the third. Harris subsequently grabbed a crucial defensive rebound and hit a pair of game-sealing free throws.

And against the Wildcats, free-throw disparity was the big story. Kentucky fouled an Indiana three-point shooter a staggering four times en route to the Hoosiers going 28-for-31 from the charity stripe compared to UK's 3-for-7 mark. Indiana cruised to victory despite not even shooting 40 percent from the field.

The last time Indiana won back-to-back games away from home against KenPom top 75 competition was during the 2022 Big Ten tournament. As a result, they have one of the best Wins Above Bubble marks in the country, at least as far as Torvik WAB is concerned.

Though it was a great week for the Hoosier State, the same cannot be said for the state of Michigan.

Michigan State got completely shut down at Tennessee, making just nine field goals in a 15-point loss. The Spartans were our No. 3 overall seed last week, but we had to bump them from the top seed line for that one.

Four days later, Michigan took its second loss of the year. The reigning national champions went to Villanova and failed to make the most of all the second chances that came from 20 offensive rebounds. They simply couldn't get stops in the "third quarter" as Villanova stretched a five-point halftime lead into an insurmountable 17-point margin. We're keeping them comfortably in the field for now, but the Players Era 16 might change that.

12 Teams in the Projected Field : 3. Florida, 9. Vanderbilt, 11. Tennessee, 12. Texas, 13. Alabama, 17. LSU, 21. Texas A&M, 27. Georgia, 31. Missouri, 33. Arkansas, 37. Ole Miss, 43. Auburn

Biggest Development : Tennessee Clamps Down on Defense

Over the past few years, Rick Barnes kept pulling one of the best scorers in the nation out of the portal. Ja'Kobi Gillespie averaged 18.4 PPG for Tennessee last season. Chaz Lanier went for 18.0 PPG in 2024-25. And the year before that was when Dalton Knecht came out of nowhere for 21.7 points per game.

This year, though, it appears the Volunteers are getting back to their roots as a terrorizing defense.

Michigan State shot 9-for-50 from the field as Tennessee held the Spartans below 50 points for the first time since that historically embarrassing 67-37 loss at Rutgers in January 2021. That already remarkable result was made all the more impressive by coming on the heels of Michigan State's convincing win over Duke in the Champions Classic.

The Volunteers followed up that 61-46 victory with a 78-51 trouncing of Coastal Carolina. It would have been their third time holding an opponent below 50 points were it not for JT Kelsheimer's important-to-some three-pointer at the buzzer.

For the year, opponents are shooting 30.2 percent on two-point attempts against Tennessee, and 27.1 percent overall. In both departments, the Volunteers are leading the nation by a slightly absurd margin.

They will play in the Players Era 16 this week, opening with Maryland on Tuesday. If the bracket holds to form and they run into Iowa State in the semifinals before a championship game against either St. John's or Texas Tech, buckle up for some physical races to 60 points.

Mid-Majors Summary (A-10, AAC, MVC, MWC, P12, WCC)

8 Teams in the Projected Field : 18. Gonzaga, 29. Memphis, 34. Utah State, 42. Grand Canyon, 44. Saint Mary's, 45. VCU, 55. Wichita State, 57. Murray State

Also Considered : Saint Louis, Santa Clara, San Diego State, Texas State, Oregon State

Biggest Development : Saint Mary's Hands Saint Louis a Second Straight Loss

'Twas a rough mid-November for the Saint Louis Billikens.

Hopes of adding super senior Robbie Avila to the mix went out the door when he transferred to TCU on Nov. 12.

A few days later, they suffered a rare, low-scoring home loss to High Point. They averaged 93.6 points per game at home last season and had just dropped 125 on Northern Kentucky five days prior to hosting the Panthers, but they couldn't buy a bucket in that 68-58 loss.

And in their lone game of the past seven days, a road trip to Moraga went horribly awry, as Saint Mary's shot 37-for-38 on free-throw attempts on its way to a 17-point victory. The Billikens looked like the better team early on, but all those fouls proved to be their undoing.

All of a sudden, that opening-week, neutral-site victory over Missouri is less of a testament to this team's second-weekend potential and more of a "the only reason they're still on our at-large radar" result.

Conversely, what a big win for the Gaels, who had a tough overtime loss at Nevada earlier this month.

They're just getting warmed up on their nonconference schedule, though. They have a gigantic game coming up against UCLA on Thanksgiving, followed by either Georgetown or Texas on Friday. They'll also play at Oklahoma State and at New Mexico in December before beginning their journey through a Gonzaga-less WCC.

If you haven't watched the Gaels yet this season, be forewarned that they definitely aren't the grind-it-out, win-with-defense team of yore. With Mickey McConnell taking Randy Bennett's place at head coach this summer, they've already scored 90 points in a game more times (six) than they did in the previous two seasons combined (four).

Fun fact: The last time Saint Mary's scored at least 90 points in five games in a season was 2009-10—when McConnell and Matthew Dellavedova were co-running the offense. And it's not even Thanksgiving yet. It's a new era of Gaels hoops.

21 Teams in the Projected Field : 38. High Point, 56. UC Santa Barbara, 58. Wright State, 59. Miami (OH), 60. Western Kentucky, 61. UNC Wilmington, 62. Montana State, 63. McNeese, 64. James Madison, 65. Furman, 66. Columbia, 67. St. Thomas, 68. Central Arkansas, 69. American, 70. Howard, 71. Vermont, 72. Queens, 73. Bethune-Cookman, 74. Tennessee State, 75. Siena, 76. Long Island

Biggest Development : UC Santa Barbara Stays Undefeated

Already, the list of teams with a zero in the loss column has been whittled down to just 37.

Among the teams in this tier, only six are still standing: High Point (who legitimately might not lose during the regular season), UC Santa Barbara, Wright State, Utah Valley, Missouri State and—wonderfully enough, if you have any memories of last season—Miami-Ohio.

We've highlighted both High Point and Wright State in this section in prior weeks, and today we're giving UC Santa Barbara its flowers.

Led by 22 points from Saint Mary's and UConn transfer Aidan Mahaney, the Gauchos improved to 5-0 with a nice road win over Pepperdine this past Thursday. They also took care of business at home against Nevada the previous week, already winning what were probably their two toughest nonconference games.

They do play a rigorous 22-game Big West schedule, though, including challenging road games against Utah Valley, UC Irvine and UC San Diego. It's almost inevitable that they're going to take some L's at some point.

But if you've been wondering who the best three-point-shooting team is this season, it has thus far been UCSB, sitting at 55-for-119 (46.2%).

Mahaney is 11-for-20. Teammates Viljami Vartiainen and Antonio Chol are 11-for-21 and 9-for-13, respectively. Against D-I opponents, the Gauchos have taken more than half of their field-goal attempts from beyond the arc, making nearly half of them.

And if they keep making it rain like that, I'm going to be very tempted to pick them to pull off at least one upset in the Dance.

articles.title: 1 Trade Every NBA Team Would Make If the Trade Deadline Were Today
articles.summary: NBA trade season can technically tip off at any time, but its unofficial starting points aren't here yet.
articles.body:
NBA trade season can technically tip off at any time, but its unofficial starting points aren't here yet.

Teams haven't reached the first-quarter mark that always gets held up as a true barometer for what they can and can't do. And the trade-eligible player pool remains weeks away from that mid-December splash of most free agents signed this offseason.

In other words, front offices have no obvious incentives to broker trades any time soon. Unless, of course, we put a hypothetical one in front of them, like, say, a fast-pass path to the trade deadline.

If teams had to act right now—based on the information they have, but also free of the trade restrictions that will lift between now and the Feb. 11 cutoff—which direction would they take? Let's break out the crystal ball and build some logical trade concepts to find out.

ATL | BKN | BOS | CHA | CHI | CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GSW | HOU | IND | LAC | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN | NOP | NYK | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX | POR | SAC | SAS | TOR | UTA | WAS

The trade: CJ McCollum, Asa Newell and a future first-round pick to the Bulls for Norman Powell and Jalen Smith

The Hawks need more creation and shot-making in their half-court offense. They could use more size, spacing and glass-cleaning at the center spot.

This deal could deliver both—at a price far below what would bust the piggy bank.

Powell has an All-Star selection on his resume and is in possession of a third consecutive 20-point scoring average. Smith is setting a host of personal-bests while also splashing 41.1 percent of his long-range looks.

The on-court upgrades they would provide could make up for the losses of McCollum (playing less than last season), Newell (lost for multiple months following toe surgery) and a non-premium first-round pick (maybe the 2028 selection that would be the lesser of Cleveland's or Utah's).

The trade: Mitchell Robinson, Sam Hauser and multiple first-round picks to the Pelicans for Trey Murphy III

Alarm sirens might be sounding amid Boston's four-game losing streak, lowlighted by consecutive losses to the Kings and Steph Curry-less Warriors. This isn't, however, a recommendation for a panic trade.

In fact, it's the total opposite. It's an aggressive wager on the sustainability of the hot start that preceded this downturn and a chance to make this group better right now and moving forward by winning the Murphy sweepstakes.

Two first-round picks feels like it should be enough, even if New Orleans is adamant that it's not . But Boston has internal replacements for both Robinson (Chris Cenac Jr., Luka Garza) and Hauser (Baylor Scheierman, Hugo González), and it needs Murphy's length, athleticism, shot-making and support scoring to become a more credible contending threat.

The trade: Michael Porter Jr., Keon Ellis and two first-round picks to the Magic for Paolo Banchero, Goga Bitadze and Jase Richardson

The Nets need a directional change in the worst kind of way. This was, ostensibly, supposed to be the season that started leading them back to winning ways. Instead, they're routinely getting clobbered and feeling as far removed from relevance as ever.

Pivoting toward something— anything —else seems overdue. With such little locked down for the long haul, assuming the challenge of tailoring a roster around Banchero seems as interesting an option as any.

The No. 1 pick in 2022 offers a potentially special blend of size, strength and skill, a combo that has already crowned him as a Rookie of the Year and an NBA All-Star (as a sophomore, no less). The gravity he'd bring as a go-to option with a powerful downhill game could make life a lot easier on building blocks Egor Dëmin and Mikel Brown Jr.

The trade: Dennis Schröder, Grant Williams, Tidjane Salaün, a first-round pick and two second-round picks to the Pelicans for Zion Williamson

The Hornets have been searching for offensive answers since their summer split from LaMelo Ball. And, no, they shouldn't just plan on finding them from a healthy Kon Knueppel (whenever they see him again).

Adding Williamson would give them more purpose on the offensive end. More finishing force at the basket, too. And more free-throw volume, as well, adding to the list of possible needs filled with this transaction.

Williamson, who was born in North Carolina and raised in South Carolina, would arrive with some LaMelo-like availability risks, but he'd also bring a similar wow factor (and a ton of numbers) on the offensive end. If the Hornets could add him for a single first-round pick—maybe the lottery-protected first they're owed by the Heat—and, effectively, filler, they'd jump on it.

The trade: Norman Powell and Jalen Smith to the Rockets for Reed Sheppard and Steven Adams

The Bulls essentially signed Powell to become their top trade chip. They should be pleasantly surprised to see Smith sitting not too far behind.

Trade season is the perfect time to cash out these stocks. Turning them into Sheppard and all of his offensive-mastery, defense-bending potential is exactly the kind of move a rebuilder needs to make.

The Bulls badly need a young backcourt shooter to slot alongside Caleb Wilson, Matas Buzelis and Josh Giddey. Sheppard could be tremendous in that role, and his offensive production could pop in a more development-focused environment than Houston.

The trade: Jarrett Allen to the Hornets for Naz Reid and Ryan Kalkbrenner

Look, this might be a more dramatic move than what the Cavaliers would actually make, but the longer they're just treading water, the more likely it seems that something major is coming. And a major something would almost certainly involve Allen, who is objectively both a good player and a not-great frontcourt fit with Evan Mobley.

Cleveland would be trading away the most talented player here, but it might emerge with a more cohesive roster and a better frontcourt rotation.

The Cavs could slide Mobley into the 5 spot and use Reid, a career 36.9 percent three-point shooter, to clear up congestion around the basket. They'd still have double-big protection behind their guards, only without the logistical issues on offense. They'd also have a wealth of reserve options at center, freeing them to flip Thomas Bryant or even Kalkbrenner to one of the many win-now suitors in that market.

The trade: Kyrie Irving to the Jazz for Ace Bailey, Brice Sensabaugh, Jusuf Nurkić and a first-round pick

The Mavs might be doing what they can to quiet trade chatter around Irving, but it will not be silenced. One of the latest rumblings involved the Jazz giving Irving "internal consideration," per SNY's Ian Begley .

That's a surprising—and, frankly, strange—suitor, but it's one Dallas should welcome, because the Mavericks' public resistance to engaging in Irving trade discussions suggests it might take an overpay to get a deal done.

This should clear that bar. Bailey is still carving his spot in this league, but 2025's fifth overall pick could form a fascinating long-term frontcourt combo with Cooper Flagg.

Sensabaugh offers his own keeper potential as a quick-strike scorer, and any first-round pick could deliver something substantial. Nurkić, meanwhile, could be rerouted elsewhere for an additional asset or two.

The trade: Zeke Nnaji, Julian Strawther and a second-round pick to the Clippers for Kris Dunn

Stop us if you've heard this one before, but Denver could really use some depth. And defense.

Dunn could scratch both itches, and he should fit the Nuggets' limited trade budget (especially if there are Strawther fans in the Clippers front office).

Dunn would immediately serve as this team's best backcourt stopper, and the more time he spent with the Nuggets' stars, the easier time he'd have helping out as a screener, stationary shooter and secondary playmaker. As an added bonus, this would help the Nuggets duck below the dreaded second-apron line.

The trade: Duncan Robinson, John Collins, Ron Holland II and a future first-round pick to the Mavericks for Kyrie Irving

Of all realistic trade candidates, Irving seems most likely to have a direct impact on this season's championship race. Especially if he finds his way to Detroit, where the Pistons have standing needs for secondary creation, scoring, shooting and high-pressure playoff experience.

Detroit has to tread a little carefully after tying up so much of its finances into the Cade Cunningham-Ausar Thompson-Jalen Duren trio. The Pistons will need young, cost-controlled talent (or the means of acquiring it) to sustain a contending-caliber roster under this collective bargaining agreement.

The Pistons cannot, in other words, afford to extend a blank-check type of offer to the Mavericks. But if something more reasonable like this could get it done, then you've probably entered no-brainer territory for Detroit.

The trade: Kristaps Porziņģis, Moses Moody and two future first-round picks to the Pelicans for Trey Murphy III and Yves Missi

The Warriors might have the appetite to go even bigger , but in a perfect world, they'd find a significant on-court upgrade without sacrificing either Jimmy Butler or Draymond Green. And, ideally, they'd find that upgrade in someone young enough to contribute both now and into the post-Stephen Curry era.

This deal would allow all of the above—and even add some more size and springs to their center collection.

It's on the lighter end of what New Orleans reportedly wants, but this is probably as high as Golden State would go for a non-star. Murphy is a turbo-charged version of Moody's best-case scenario, and Missi's rim-running would be a welcome addition to a center group that lacked a great backup plan behind Porziņģis.

The trade: Reed Sheppard to the Grizzlies for Ty Jerome

Fred VanVleet's return more or less solved the puzzle for Houston's offense. It also limited Sheppard's role and almost certainly knocked him out of his comfort zone.

Maybe the Rockets are willing to wait and see whether 2024's No. 3 pick can turn things around. Or perhaps the win-now possibilities are too great for Houston to afford any more growing pains.

Buying big on Jerome's breakout would add home-run power to a reserve Rockets unit struggling for consistency ( 23rd in offensive efficiency). And, honestly, if Jerome sustains his sizzling start (24.8 points, 5.3 assists), he could even give Houston some change-of-pace optionality at point guard come playoff time.

The trade: Jarace Walker, Ben Sheppard and Jay Huff to the Clippers for Brook Lopez and Gradey Dick

Things have gotten late awfully early in the Circle City, as the Pacers' planned return to relevance hasn't taken flight. But their play with Tyrese Haliburton on the floor (plus-9.7 net differential, per Cleaning the Glass ) offers hope of a turnaround if he can get past this hamstring injury.

Assuming Indy agrees with that assessment, the aim should still be on plugging roster holes around him. Adding a serviceable center behind Ivica Zubac and wing shooters might share top-billing status on the to-do list.

Lopez, who backed up Zubac for the first half of last season, would stabilize the backup 5 role while adding a spacing-and-shot-blocking combo unseen since Myles Turner skipped town. Dick is more of a hope-for-the-best dart throw, but as a 6'7" wing with a 48 percent splash rate so far, the hope isn't totally blind.

The trade: Brook Lopez and Gradey Dick to the Pacers for Jarace Walker, Ben Sheppard and Jay Huff

Yes, folks, this is the same package pitched for the Pacers. But it just feels like an obvious win for both sides.

While the Pacers have reasons to believe they can salvage their season, the Clippers have incentive to prioritize the future. They're on the hunt for draft capital , but young players with growth potential might serve the same purpose.

Walker, who just turned 23 in September, seems like a great second-draft candidate as someone who could be a scenery change away from finding his footing. And Sheppard, 25, has flashed both three-and-D abilities and a pinch of playmaking.

The trade: Kevon Looney and a second-round pick to the Bucks for Jericho Sims

If the Lakers could turn a second-round pick into Sims, he'd be on the roster already . But a second-round offer was reasonable then and remains reasonable now, maybe even more so with Milwaukee giving him sporadic floor time.

Sims is worth something, though, particularly to the Lakers. They "have already decided that Kevon Looney isn't a workable backup center," per The Athletic's Dan Woike , and also have "limited trade assets" to fill the void.

Sims has a limited skillset, but he's a big, bouncy center, which makes him an easy stylistic fit for this Luka Dončić-driven offense. More than 95 percent of Sims' field goals last season were dunks or layups.

The trade: Jerami Grant and two first-round picks to the Pelicans for Trey Murphy III

It's tempting to push an idea of flipping Ty Jerome for future assets. The idea of any 29-year-old orchestrating a career year invites skepticism. And even if Memphis believes the breakout is real, it could still question his timeline fit with one of the league's youngest rosters .

But that train of thinking gets derailed quickly on Beale Street, where Memphis has shown enough promise to—at least temporarily—buy into the fun. Especially if doing so meant bringing back someone like Murphy, who can help this club right now and for years to come.

The Grizzlies have some of the best depth in basketball. There may not be a great player on the roster ( yet—Cameron Boozer's leaps could be galactical with time ), but there is an abundance of above-average to good ones. Murphy would expand that collection and still has the chance to enter very-good territory with better offensive numbers in a winning environment.

The trade: Dru Smith and a first-round pick swap to the Grizzlies for Cam Spencer

Miami has flashed plenty of resolve and resilience while wiggling out of a listless 0-4 start to embark upon a seven-game winning streak (and counting). It still hasn't quieted the big-picture concerns about the quality of its guard group.

"The belief of several scouts and executives polled by ESPN is that the Heat lack the supporting cast around [Giannis] Antetokounmpo and [Bam] Adebayo to make a deep playoff run," Tim MacMahon reported. "The strong starts by [Davion] Mitchell and [Klay] Thompson haven't swayed the opinions that Miami will need to upgrade its starting backcourt before being a legitimate threat to come out of the East."

Trading for Spencer wouldn't quiet the skeptics, but it would address needs for more ball-handlers who don't spoil the spacing. He may not be a headline reason why things are going so great for the Grizzlies, but his 55/54.1/96 shooting slash and 3.9 assists-per-turnover are significant parts of the winning formula.

The trade: Myles Turner to the Warriors for Kristaps Porziņģis, Moses Moody and a future first-round pick swap

The Bucks tipped off their roster reset with this summer's Giannis Antetokounmpo blockbuster, but they still have a handful of carryover veterans they'd love to flip for future assets.

Turner tops that list, even though his sagging production and escalating earnings make him tricky (if not impossible) to trade for even neutral assets. That unicorn's horn doesn't quite fit the same when he's misfiring on nearly 75 percent of his perimeter shots.

But if the Bucks could sniff out a desperate suitor—say, a club whose starting (and $20 million) center stepped away from basketball —maybe they could stumble into something like this, delivering financial relief, draft capital and a 24-year-old wing. The Warriors have dismissed this possibility for now, but the Bucks should be ready to pounce upon any inkling of a mindset shift.

The trade: Isaiah Evans to the Suns for Rasheer Fleming

With the Wolves poised to get Anthony Edwards back at some point and proving plenty feisty without him, they can afford to focus on more niche needs. Having some usable size off the bench behind Joan Beringer and Trey Lyles would be helpful.

Now, is Fleming actually usable? The Suns don't seem to think so, but they're also a little infamous for their unique player evaluations. ( Who else was coughing up an unprotected future first for Miles Bridges? ) Fleming has barely played at this level, but his tools say he's worth the investment.

He has length, athleticism and ample defensive versatility. His pre-draft report labeled him as a floor-spacing, rim-rattling play-finisher, too, meaning if Minnesota could coax that back out of him, it would have a great pick-and-roll partner to pair with Edwards or LaMelo Ball in the screen game.

The trade: Dejounte Murray to the Suns for Jalen Green

The Pelicans should probably be focused on brokering bigger deals for draft assets, but if they could get anything done right now, it would almost certainly be finding a resolution to the Dejounte drama .

He wants out, and New Orleans would pack his bags if it could sniff out a taker. Phoenix seems an obvious destination given its playmaking shortage and limited trade budget. The Pels are just waiting for the Suns to admit as much.

Would Green fare any better with this group? Who knows, but he is younger, more athletic and, you know, not angling for a way out of New Orleans. There are certainly less interesting developmental projects for the Pels to put on their to-do list.

The trade: Pacôme Dadiet and three second-round picks to the Pelicans for Karlo Matković

Would the Knicks prefer using this opportunity to clean up their financial books? They better hope not. Not if they want any shot at defending their throne, at least.

And in case this isn't obvious, throne-defending should absolutely be the aim here. Throw out the club's wobbly ( hungover? ) 0-3 start, and this is a .786 team with a top-five net rating .

Big swings aren't needed, but backup bigs sure are. And Matković is quietly one of the more intriguing ones around. He's a 6'10", 231-pounder with an ignitable outside shot (career 37.2 percent) and above-the-rim ups.

The trade: Nikola Topić to the Celtics for Hugo González

With its injury report reading more like a novella, OKC has had its depth pushed beyond the breaking point. Wing depth might be the biggest need, other than maybe a time machine to go back and erase those salary-focused subtractions that defined their offseason.

González could be a fun get. He's still in the figuring-things-out portion of his maturation, but he has good size for the wings (6'6", 200 lbs) and a great motor without an off switch.

He could fit the defensive scheme right now and hustle his way to some play-finishing chances with all of the disruption OKC creates. And with Bennett Stirtz proving such a quick study, the Thunder should have no hesitation about losing Topić.

The trade: Paolo Banchero, Goga Bitadze and Jase Richardson to the Nets for Michael Porter Jr., Keon Ellis and two first-round picks

Have the Magic seen enough to know that the Banchero-Franz Wagner pairing just isn't the right fit for either one? They'd never admit that publicly, of course, because they'd torpedo their own trade leverage by doing so, but Orlando's issues go way beyond its rough luck with the injury bug.

There's too much overlap in both strengths and weaknesses between Banchero and Wagner. And if it's even possible to put enough playmaking and perimeter shooting around them to paper over that redundancy, Orlando isn't close to doing it. Oh, and this club also happens to have the payroll of a win-right-this-second contender.

The Magic would be better off picking a lane, and they have to like what they've seen of late from Wagner as an aggressive two-way playmaker. He'd have a much easier time slotting alongside a big-time shotmaker like Porter, and Orlando would gain some needed flexibility to help with either finding cheap contributors or facilitating more moves.

The trade: Justin Edwards and three second-round picks to the Pelicans for Yves Missi

Any significant addition would require some boat-rocking. With the Sixers already scrambling to find their respective comfort zones and facing a loudly ticking clock, a notable shakeup seems unlikely—even if analytics are less sold on this squad than their record would indicate.

A targeted move for a role-playing reserve could be in the cards, though, especially given the obvious need for reliable depth behind 41-year-old LeBron James and 96-appearances-over-the-last-three-seasons Joel Embiid.

Missi could be a solid get, provided the Pelicans actually put a reasonable asking price on him. With his length and bounce, he could shine as an above-the-rim finisher with (much) better playmakers around him than he's had in New Orleans.

The trade: Jalen Green to the Pelicans for Dejounte Murray

Again, this trade feels too obvious not to happen. And if things fast-forwarded to the deadline, maybe market silence around the players involved could fully convince these front offices this is the best they can do for their guard trade candidates.

In real life, of course, they haven't reached that point. The two teams have talked, but "nothing even remotely close to a deal is happening," per The Athletic's Sam Amick .

That should change. If Phoenix's aim is finding a better backcourt fit for Devin Booker, it's hard to argue against Murray. Assuming he could perk back up in a more competitive environment, he has shown a better penchant for passing and defense and even been a more efficient scorer than Green.

The trade: Scoot Henderson to the Clippers for Rui Hachimura

The Blazers have no reason to rush into anything. They've had their share of signature wins and zero bad losses. Ja Morant had really encouraging flashes before a hamstring injury stunted his run, and the guard-heavy look did nothing to stall the All-Star ascension of Deni Avdija.

Trading Henderson wouldn't require rushing anything, though. They have taken their time in hopes of getting things right with the 2023 draft's No. 3 pick, but it just hasn't clicked. In fact, things are trending in the wrong direction, with Henderson struggling more than anyone amid the backcourt logjam.

If L.A. wanted a crack at Henderson— and given all of the obstacles in its future, why wouldn't it? —then Portland could turn his perceived potential into tangible production and reliable depth at forward with Hachimura. He's shooting better than 40 percent from range for the fourth consecutive season, and he cleared 50 percent from the field the previous three campaigns, too.

The trade: Domantas Sabonis to the Nets for Mo Wagner, Terance Mann, Drake Powell and a protected future first-round pick

Sabonis has been on the trade block for ages . Sacramento clearly wants to have something to show for moving its stat sheet-stuffer, even if the market has routinely shown its skepticism about his ability to author postseason success.

This would allow the Kings to have a few somethings to show their fans. Never mind that the pick would be far from the best in the Nets' collection, that Powell has lost some luster as a prospect or that Wagner and Mann would be temporary NorCal residents.

A first-round pick is still a first-round pick. Powell remains a relentless defender with top-notch tools. Wagner and Mann could both have value if turned back to the trade market. It's not a haul, but it's a chance for Sacramento to feel like it got some real stuff back.

The trade: Carter Bryant, a future first-round pick and two second-round picks to the Raptors for Collin Murray-Boyles

There is a spicier pitch to build around a De'Aaron Fox deal. If the Spurs ever seriously explore that route, they won't do it midseason.

What they might do, though, is seek out an energetic forward who can defend, finish and handle the dirty-work duties alongside Victor Wembanyama.

Murray-Boyles offers do-it-all versatility on defense and quick, smart ball-moving on offense. Plus reliable finishing, which would only grow more impactful alongside San Antonio's wealth of shot-creators.

The trade: Immanuel Quickley, Jakob Poeltl, Ja'Kobe Walter and two first-round picks to the Mavericks for Kyrie Irving and Daniel Gafford

If the Raptors are getting a healthy Kawhi Leonard back sooner than later, then their wildest hopes and dreams for this season are all still achievable.

They just might want to get greedy about adding a third star to the mix, especially someone who can fill existing voids for creation, shooting and isolation bucket-getting.

Oh, and as long as Toronto is getting greedy, it might as well get out of Poeltl's contract while adding a more reliable—and more impactful—center in Gafford.

A closing five of Irving, Leonard, Gafford, Scottie Barnes and RJ Barrett could have the Raptors ready for whatever the playoffs throw at them.

The trade: Jusuf Nurkić, Josh Green, Kyle Filipowski and two first-round picks to the Cavaliers for Jarrett Allen and Nae'Qwan Tomlin

Did the Jazz lose this season before it ever really started? Maybe, but they feel too pot-committed to this core to abandon hope, especially if they could land someone like Allen with staying power, who's signed at relatively reasonable rates through 2028-29.

They would need much better luck on the health front, obviously, but an Allen-Lauri Markkanen-Jaren Jackson Jr. frontcourt could still be a game-changer. Plus, they would have all of the defensive protection needed to explore all of the offensive possibilities of a perimeter rotation featuring Keyonte George, Darryn Peterson and Ace Bailey.

The trade: Anthony Davis to the Warriors for Draymond Green, Kristaps Porziņģis, Moses Moody, a future first-round pick and a future first-round pick swap

Maybe the Wizards would disagree, but if they have a chance to flip Davis for assets and flexibility, they should probably take it.

Even when ESPN's Brian Windhorst recently relayed that Davis isn't "looking for a max extension," he did note that the 10-time All-Star is "looking for a lot of money."

Washington should want no part of paying that. Davis is a dubious big-dollar contract candidate on his own as a 33-year-old with a detailed injury history, but this nears (or barrels into) nonstarter territory considering how far this club might be removed from winning.

The Wizards would never see Porziņģis and may have the briefest relationship with Green, and they could still come out ahead. Avoiding a cap-crushing overpay for Davis might be that valuable. And don't sleep on Moody as a long-term keeper, nor on the value of future draft assets from a franchise with as much uncertainty as Golden State.

articles.title: 5 NBA Teams Already Regretting Their 2026 Draft Picks
articles.summary: The 2026-27 NBA season is still fairly young, but that doesn't mean there aren't a few teams already feeling buyers' remorse when looking back at the 2026 draft.
articles.body:
The 2026-27 NBA season is still fairly young, but that doesn't mean there aren't a few teams already feeling buyers' remorse when looking back at the 2026 draft.

This could either mean that their current rookie is underperforming, a player who went later in the draft has been better than expected or positional needs have changed now a month-ish into the season.

These are five teams already regretting their 2026 first-round pick.

Sacramento Kings Selecting Alex Karaban at No. 29

This is a double-doozie of a bad pick by the Sacramento Kings, who not only selected the struggling Karaban in the first round but also traded up to do so.

The Cleveland Cavaliers were originally at 29, yet the Kings wanted Karaban's size and shooting on the wing enough to give up a future second-round pick to move up from No. 34 to grab the former UConn standout.

While No. 7 overall pick Darius Acuff Jr. has been an instant success (25.4 points, 7.4 assists per game), Karaban has struggled to begin his NBA career despite turning 24 a few weeks ago.

Shooting just 18.2 percent overall in his first seven games over 82 total minutes is alarming given his age and college experience. While most of his court time has come in limited doses, Karaban played 29 minutes in a loss to the Oklahoma City Thunder on Nov. 15, going 0-of-3 from the field for zero points. His per-36 minute stat line of 3.1 points, 4.4 rebounds, 1.3 assists and 0.0 blocks doesn't look real.

To make matters worse, the Cavs ended up taking shooting guard Meleek Thomas with the Kings' original pick at 34, as the 20-year-old looks like the steal of the draft right now. He's averaging 12.7 points, 1.4 steals and is shooting 42.0 percent from three primarily as a reserve.

A teammate of Acuff at Arkansas, Thomas could have been the perfect long-term answer at shooting guard for a 2-14 Kings team desperate for young talent.

Chicago Bulls Selecting Dailyn Swain at No. 15

Caleb Wilson looks like a future star, as the No. 4 overall pick has finally given the Chicago Bulls a prospect worth building around.

The same cannot be said for Dailyn Swain, who was selected 11 spots later.

Following a big year at Texas, Swain had a dismal summer league showing in Las Vegas, averaging just 4.2 points on 12.9 percent shooting in 28.0 minutes across four games. The NBA hasn't been an easy transition, either, as he has failed to crack Chicago's rotation and has bounced back and forth from the G League.

In 27 total NBA minutes this year, Swain has recorded just seven points, five rebounds and two assists, going 2-of-9 (22.2 percent) from the floor and 0-of-5 from three with four turnovers.

Caleb Wilson's hand injury could create a short-term opportunity for Swain, but his longer-term path to playing time looks crowded, with Matas Buzelis, Isaac Okoro, Patrick Williams, Noa Essengue, Leonard Miller and others competing for minutes in Chicago.

Shooting guard Bennett Stirtz, taken one pick after Swain by the Oklahoma City Thunder, is making 46.4 percent of his threes in a rotation role right now. There are a number of guards and big men taken later in the first round who would have made more sense for this Chicago roster as well.

Swain looks like a bad fit and has clearly struggled to make the adjustment to the NBA thus far. Hopefully a bigger role with the Windy City Bulls can help him find his ideal role in Chicago.

Charlotte Hornets Selecting Hannes Steinbach at No. 14

Hannes Steinbach could carve out a role as an elite rebounder in the NBA, as the 6'11" big man has an active motor, strong frame and good instincts.

Was he really needed on this Charlotte Hornets team, however?

Moussa Diabaté took over as Hornets' starting center a year ago and has thrived as one of the NBA's best glass cleaners. His 5.5 offensive rebounds per game and 19.6 offensive rebound percentage both rank No. 1 overall in the league this season. At age 24, he's either the long-term answer at center for Charlotte or at worst a key backup.

Last year's 34th overall pick, Ryan Kalkbrenner, has also proved himself to be rotation worthy (10.6 rebounds and 2.2 blocks per 36 minutes this season) and is a towering figure at 7'1".

So, where does this leave Steinbach, especially with Naz Reid playing a big frontcourt role as well?

For now, he's logged most of his court time with the G League's Greensboro Swarm. Steinbach has played just 63 total minutes across five games for the Hornets, scoring a total of 14 points on 43.8 percent shooting overall.

Yes, his selection was made before LaMelo Ball was traded, although clearly conversations were happening given the timing of the deal. The Hornets should have focused on point guard help in the draft and not drafting a third center, especially not with their lottery pick.

1 Trade Every NBA Team Would Make Today 🧠

Dallas Mavericks Selecting Morez Johnson Jr. at No. 9

This may have been the Dallas Mavericks' best (and perhaps, only) shot to pair an elite prospect alongside Cooper Flagg given the amount of draft capital going out over the next several years.

For now, the selection of Michigan forward Morez Johnson Jr. at No. 9 overall has been underwhelming.

New Mavs coach Dusty May, Johnson's coach at Michigan, claimed he didn't know who Dallas was going to draft and that he was "shocked" when the 20-year-old ended up being the selection.

Both of Johnson's former Michigan teammates, Yaxel Lendeborg (19.2 points, 7.4 rebounds, 3.6 assists) and Aday Mara (10.1 points, 7.1 rebounds, 1.7 blocks), are off to terrific starts to their careers despite being taken 11th and 12th overall. It's only fair to mention that both are older than Johnson, who's currently playing through a left shin contusion.

Still, modest averages of 6.3 points and 4.7 rebounds on 23.5 percent shooting from three are disappointing, especially when others drafted after him have been far more productive.

Dallas didn't really need another forward, with guard play being the biggest weakness on the roster. Brayden Burries would have been a strong fit between Kyrie Irving and Flagg with his all-around play and has already hit double-digit scoring figures in 10 games thus far. He went one draft pick after Johnson, No. 10 overall to the Milwaukee Bucks.

Johnson has been fine, but there were other, better options available.

Brooklyn Nets Selecting Mikel Brown Jr. at No. 6

Darius Acuff Jr. has been the best rookie in the NBA so far this season and should have a number of teams second-guessing whether they made the right choice by letting him slide to No. 7 overall.

The biggest guilty party? The Brooklyn Nets.

Brooklyn desperately needs a star to build around. Maybe Brown turns out to be the guy one day, but for now he's primarily come off the bench and is shooting a measly 36.5 percent from two and 33.8 percent from three to begin his NBA career.

The Nets started guards such as Keon Ellis and Nolan Traoré ahead of Brown. The No. 6 overall pick finally made his first start in a 142-116 loss to the Minnesota Timberwolves on Nov. 23, in Brooklyn's 16th game of the season.

Brown could end up having a good career, but Acuff's talent is clearly on another level.

The Sacramento Kings point guard was handed the keys to the offense immediately and is averaging 25.4 points, 3.6 rebounds and 7.4 assists with a swing rating of plus-4.3 to begin his career. Brown is at 12.0 points, 1.7 rebounds, 3.5 assists with a swing rating of minus-11.3 for the Nets.

This is meant more as praise for Acuff than a knock on Brown. Acuff was exactly the type of player Brooklyn needed to be the new face of the franchise, however, and could have been paired with 6'8" Egor Dëmin, the No. 8 overall pick in the draft last year.

articles.title: NCAA ends mandatory off-day media access before the women’s Elite Eight but keeps it for men
articles.summary: The NCAA no longer requires women's teams to hold press conferences between the Sweet 16 and Elite Eight, while men's teams still must do both.
articles.body: The NCAA will no longer require women’s teams to hold a news conference or open their locker rooms to reporters on the day between the Sweet 16 and the Elite Eight. Each school can decide whether to make its coaches and players available. Men’s teams playing for a spot in the Final Four still have to do both. The Division I Women’s Basketball Committee announced the change July 10. NCAA vice president Lynn Holzman spelled it out in a Nov. 20 memo to schools obtained by USA TODAY Sports. The committee said it had heard from coaches and players about tournament obligations and wanted to cut both the time teams spend on them and the access they have to give reporters. COLLEGE BASKETBALL GETS A NEW NO. 1 AS THREE TEAMS FALL OUT OF THE AP TOP FIVE IN A SINGLE WEEK It’s the biggest event of the year, and it should take up all your time. In the NIL era, players can make money off the attention that comes with being one win from the Final Four. They can spare a few minutes for reporters, and I’ve got a question for them that has nothing to do with tomorrow’s game. Did any of you actually ask the NCAA to make these sessions optional? The NCAA puts eight teams at each women’s regional site and four at each men’s site. Last March, Geno Auriemma said UConn had to be at the arena around 6 a.m. for a shootaround before a 4 p.m. game. If that’s the problem, fix the schedule. Auriemma also wanted to know why UConn had to come back for morning interviews when practice wasn’t until 6:30 that night. I’d move the interviews to practice and save everybody a trip. Why give schools the option to skip questions altogether? We just saw what an off day without media access looks like at the WNBA Finals. Neither the Dream nor the Valkyries had to leave San Francisco between Games 1 and 2, yet neither team held a media session. CBS Sports’ Lindsay Gibbs called that "pretty ridiculous." Nobody’s going to confuse Gibbs with an OutKick writer. She lists "she/her" in her X bio and called voting against North Carolina Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx "the honor of a lifetime." After Game 3, Gibbs wrote a CBS story about Angel Reese’s "contagious confidence" being her "superpower." I’d imagine the WNBA would take seven games’ worth of headlines like that, yet even Gibbs was practically begging for access. "Give us more things to talk about!!!!" she wrote. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE I had a hard enough time getting a question in when there was a news conference. Before those Finals, I’d been to dozens of news conferences and could count on two or three fingers the times I wanted to ask a question and didn’t get called on. Then I went to all 13 formal press conferences over the first three games of the Finals and got passed over every time. I’ve never had a stretch like that covering men’s sports. Nothing even comes close. When I told a WNBA rep those numbers, he gave me a lame excuse for why I wasn’t getting called on. I didn’t buy it; the league doesn’t like OutKick’s coverage and would rather hand the microphone to people whose coverage it does like. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Reese showed up for postgame questions even on nights when Atlanta hadn’t put her name on the list. Before Game 4, I finally got to ask players and coaches why both teams kept leaving the court for the national anthem, and I wanted to hear from Reese, too. Most players and coaches were available for the full 30 minutes. Reese and Dream coach Karl Smesko had to do only 15, and Atlanta’s PR staff picked who got to ask Reese a question. During the other interviews, reporters could jump in. I never got to ask her about the anthem. A couple of months earlier, the Dream had denied OutKick a credential for a game against Phoenix. The team told me it turned down 14 applications and gave priority to season credential holders and outlets that regularly covered the Dream. Atlanta also told me it considered "the tone of coverage." That leaves a beat writer in a hell of a spot. The next time the Dream deserve criticism, he knows the people he’s writing about also decide whether he gets back in the building. OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD I doubt the Chicago Sky cared for my tone in 2024 when I criticized them for using a new WNBA exemption to keep Reese and Kamilla Cardoso out of game-day shootaround interviews. Eight days earlier, I’d criticized Rory McIlroy for leaving the U.S. Open without speaking to reporters after he lost. I hear activists demand "equal pay" and "equal coverage" for female athletes all the time. Funny how I never hear those same people demand "equal criticism." I’d expect the coach of a team one win from the Final Four to take questions the day before the game. The NCAA apparently agrees, as long as it’s a men’s team.

articles.body:
With Arizona cruising to a 96-83 win over Colorado State in the Maui Invitational on Monday night, sophomore guard Bryce James saw his first action in nearly two weeks.

James wasn't afforded much time to make an impact, though, as he played a total of three minutes.

The 6'5" guard drilled a three-pointer inside the final minute of the contest with his only field-goal attempt.

Coach Tommy Lloyd had a quick hook for James. He entered at the 8:06 mark of the first half and was subbed out with just under six minutes left. He stayed on the bench until the waning moments of the second half.

James started in each of Arizona's first three games before he got the dreaded DNP-coach's decision in the 80-69 win over Auburn. Lloyd gave the impression that wouldn't be the norm moving forward.

"I wish I would have got him in the game," the coach told reporters . It's just one of those things where you get the lead playing a certain way, then they come back, and then sometimes it's hard to kind of thrust a guy into that moment when he hasn't been on the court much.

"So I kind of I went with the guys who had been out there and were able to get us that lead, and hoping they could do it again. But Bryce has really shown me a lot the last couple weeks, and we'll continue to try to find ways to give him opportunities for sure."

James once again didn't see the floor as the Wildcats outlasted UConn 85-79 the following week.

Quite simply, it doesn't look like Lloyd has a lot of faith in him. Washington transfer JJ Mandaquit supplanted James in the starting lineup beginning with the Auburn game, and Cameron Holmes is the first guard off the bench.

Arizona plays 5-1 Providence in the next round of the Maui Invitational, and a matchup with No. 19 BYU could await in Wednesday's championship. Don't be surprised if James continues to be a peripheral figure for at least the time being.

articles.title: Trae Young Slams Critics amid Career-Low Stat, 'Don't Really Care What Other People's Opinion Is'
articles.summary: In his first full season with the Washington Wizards, star guard Trae Young isn't scoring as much, but he's not concerned.
articles.body:
In his first full season with the Washington Wizards, star guard Trae Young isn't scoring as much, but he's not concerned.

While speaking to The Athletic's Josh Robbins , Young addressed his career-low average of 17.1 points per game, saying his critics don't matter as long as his team is winning.

"A lot of people may want me to shoot more, do more things, or maybe they like where I'm at," Young said. "But for me, I don't really care what other people's opinion is. I know what I'm doing right now is good for the team and good for these young guys. As we continue to win and stack games, that'll come to light and be shown more."

Wemby 'Had to Show Off' for Selena Gomez

Young's mindset appears to be paying off, as the Wizards (7-11) are riding a three-game win streak into Tuesday night's matchup against the Boston Celtics (11-6).

While Young's scoring pace may not match his days with the Atlanta Hawks, he's still an effective facilitator for a youthful Washington team. The four-time All-Star ranks third in the NBA with 8.8 assists per game.

"Obviously, I know what was expected of me when I first got here," he added. "Nobody puts more pressure on me than myself. So, I don't really let any outside voices or opinions get to me. I mean, I'm the one that's playing in the NBA. I understand what it takes to get here and what it takes to succeed in this league."

It sounds like Young will continue to prioritize winning over his individual stats, bringing some much-needed leadership to the Wizards as they try to end their perpetual rebuild.

articles.title: Pedro Martínez: "Estamos en modo supervivencia"
articles.standfirst: El entrenador del Real Madrid analiza el momento de su equipo antes de la visita del Zalgiris
articles.summary: El entrenador del Real Madrid analiza el momento de su equipo antes de la visita del Zalgiris
articles.body: Pedro Martínez, entrenador del Real Madrid de baloncesto, consideró, en la rueda de prensa previa al duelo de la Euroliga en casa contra el Zalgiris de Kaunas, que el equipo está "un poco en un modo supervivencia" y que tras no jugar la última semana como les gustaría están "más preocupados". "Esta última semana no hemos jugado como nos gustaría y estamos más preocupados. Estoy un poco en una situación difícil tratando de explicarlo, porque me niego a hablar de que nos faltan jugadores y que eso sea una excusa. No la quiero utilizar porque nuestra obligación y nuestro objetivo es ser competitivos con los jugadores que tenemos y lo están haciendo muy bien", dijo. "Estoy muy contento, y lo digo en una semana que no hemos jugado bien y que no hemos tenido buenos resultados. El equipo lo está intentando, está trabajando con buena mentalidad, pero se nos está haciendo un poco largo el no recuperar a jugadores que están llamados a ser muy importantes", prosiguió. "Hasta entonces lo que tenemos que intentar hacer es competir, apretar los dientes y mejorar en lo que dependa de nosotros para ser competitivos, porque ahora mismo estamos un poco en un modo supervivencia. No me quejo de la lucha del equipo pero ha habido algún momento en el que la impotencia nos ha podido, al ver que las cosas no nos salen como nos gustaría nos hemos un poco desmoralizado por no poder competir como nos gustaría o como hemos hecho durante bastantes partidos. Estamos en dificultades y debemos afrontarlas mirándolas a la cara", añadió. Martínez aseguró que afrontan el duelo "con toda la ilusión" y todas las ganas de hacer un buen partido "sabiendo las dificultades" que les planteará "un muy buen equipo" e indicó: "Sabemos que tenemos dificultades, han quedado claras la semana pasada, pero jugamos en casa, tenemos a nuestra afición y vamos a ser competitivos, vamos a luchar, vamos a esforzarnos. Si ganamos será una grandísima noticia, y si perdemos el camino continúa. Esto es una liga regular muy larga de 38 partidos"
